name: Hair weave

lead: A hair weave attaches wefts of human or synthetic hair to a person's own hair to add length, volume or a new style. The look changes immediately and can be kept for weeks.
Weaves are one form of artificial hair integration, alongside clip-ins, braids and wigs. Human hair is the most common choice and synthetic fibres such as Kanekalon are cheaper but less durable.

paras: In the track-and-sew method, natural hair is braided into cornrow tracks and wefts are sewn on with a needle and thread. In bonding, wefts are glued on, kept off the scalp. Clip-ins and bulk attachments are alternatives. An invisible-part sew-in takes about an hour and lasts about eight weeks.

Tight braiding or prolonged wear can cause traction alopecia and breakage. Case reports describe full-thickness scalp necrosis after tight braiding and weave placement, and an anaphylactic reaction to latex-containing hair glue. Patch-testing adhesives is commonly advised.

angle.text: A weave changes hair length, fullness and style right away, and can be kept for weeks.

lead: A hair weave, also called hair extensions or artificial hair integrations, adds human or synthetic hair to natural hair to increase length or volume or change style [1]. Wigs are related and also covered under the topic [1].

Methods include track-and-sew, where wefts are sewn onto braided cornrow tracks; bonding with glue; and clip-in or bulk attachments [1]. Wigs were fashionable in the late 17th century, while weaves appeared in the 1950s among celebrities and spread widely in the 1970s [1].
Published research consists mainly of case reports on complications: scalp injury from tight braiding with weave, and latex allergy to hair glue [2][3].
infobox: About an hour; lasts about eight weeks

paras: Track-and-sew uses a blunt needle and thread matched to hair colour; bonded wefts are glued and are often patch-tested first [1]. Human hair is the most common material, with 'tangle-free' hair chemically treated; synthetic fibres such as Kanekalon and Futura are cheaper but wear faster and are damaged by heat [1].
Tight braiding or long wear is associated with traction alopecia, breakage and follicle damage; glue has been linked to dermatitis and sensitivity [1].

A 2015 case report describes extensive full-thickness scalp loss in a young woman after tight spiral braiding and weave, needing complex reconstruction [2]. Another 2015 report describes a 29-year-old woman with airway-compromising angioedema after latex-containing hair glue was applied for a weave; glue was removed over hours with an oil-based conditioner [3].
No studies found beyond case reports of complications [2][3].
